content: Astragalus is a genus comprising approximately 2,000 species of herbs and small shrubs. These plants belong to the legume family Fabaceae and the subfamily Faboideae. They are native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Commonly, these plants are referred to as milk-vetch (for most species) or goat's-thorn (specifically for Astragalus gummifera and Astragalus tragacanthus). Some pale-flowered vetches resemble Astragalus species in appearance, but vetches tend to have a more vine-like growth habit. Astragalus species serve as food sources for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, particularly case-bearers of the genus Coleophora. Specific examples include Coleophora astragalella, which exclusively feeds on Astragalus glycyphyllos, and Coleophora cartilaginella, which feeds exclusively on Astragalus species. Other species, such as Coleophora euryaula, Coleophora gallipennella, Coleophora hippodromica, Coleophora onobrychiella, Coleophora polonicella, and Coleophora vicinella, also rely on Astragalus plants as their primary food source. Medicinal Use of Astragalus The species Astragalus membranaceus, known as huángqí (黄芪) in Chinese, has been traditionally used in Chinese medicine as a tonic herb. It is believed to act as a galactagogue and has been studied for its potential to strengthen the human immune system. The natural gum tragacanth, derived from Astragalus tragacanthus, is utilized in both pharmaceutical and textile industries. This gum is claimed to support immune function and enhance the body’s resistance to common viral infections. In Western herbal medicine, Astragalus is primarily regarded as a tonic that enhances metabolism and digestion. It is often consumed as a tea made from the plant's roots. Traditionally, it has been used to fortify the immune system and to aid in the healing of wounds and injuries. A molecule extracted from the root of Astragalus membranaceus, known as TA-65, has been identified as a telomerase activator by the biotech company Geron Corporation. TA Sciences, under a license from Geron, markets TA-65 as a nutraceutical anti-aging product at their TA Sciences Center in New York City. Traditional Uses of Huang Qi (Radix Astragali) In traditional Chinese medicine, huángqí is believed to have the following effects: It replenishes the Qi (vital energy) of the Spleen and Stomach. It promotes the ascension of Yang Qi in the Spleen and Stomach. It benefits Qi, consolidates the body’s surface, and regulates sweating. It facilitates urination and reduces swelling caused by deficiency patterns. It promotes the discharge of pus and accelerates wound healing. It tonifies and nourishes both Qi and Blood. It is used in the treatment of Wasting and Thirsting syndrome, which corresponds to diabetes in modern medical terms. Huángqí is believed to enter the Lung and Spleen meridians. Its properties are described as sweet and slightly warm. However, it is contraindicated in cases of Yin deficiency with heat or in conditions of exterior excess heat. To enhance its effects, it can be prepared with honey to tonify Spleen and Stomach Qi, with wine to tonify essence, or with salt to tonify the Kidneys. Ornamental Use Several species of Astragalus are cultivated as ornamental plants in gardens. Examples include Astragalus alpinus, which has bluish-purple flowers, Astragalus hypoglottis, which produces purple flowers, and Astragalus lotoides.
